flashcards.q: Match the symptom to the tool: crashed process, hung process, memory growth, slow-but-progressing process.
flashcards.a: Crashed -> core dump + gdb. Hung -> thread dump (jstack/jcmd, or py-spy dump for Python). Memory growth/OOM -> heap dump (jmap/jcmd) + Eclipse MAT. Slow -> live profile (py-spy record, async-profiler/JFR).

flashcards.q: What does ulimit -c default to on most systems, and what controls where the resulting core file is written?
flashcards.a: Defaults to 0 (no core dump written). ulimit -c unlimited (or systemd LimitCORE=infinity) enables it; kernel.core_pattern (/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern) controls the output location, often piped to systemd-coredump.
Yes -- jstack explicitly detects lock cycles and prints 'Found one Java-level deadlock' naming exactly which threads hold which monitors and are waiting on which others.

flashcards.q: What is retained size in a heap dump, and why is it more useful than shallow size?
flashcards.a: Retained size is the total memory that would become collectible if an object became unreachable (the object plus everything it exclusively keeps alive). A small HashMap with tiny shallow size can have massive retained size if it holds millions of entries -- retained size (via MAT's Dominator Tree) is what actually shows where memory is going.

flashcards.q: What is a cheaper first-look alternative to a full jmap heap dump, and why use it first?
flashcards.a: jmap -histo:live <pid> -- prints a live object histogram (class, instance count, bytes) without writing a full .hprof file, often enough to spot a runaway allocation without the cost (minutes, potential app impact) of a full heap dump.

flashcards.q: Why is py-spy dump considered safe to run against a live production process?
flashcards.a: It attaches from outside the process, reading the interpreter's memory via OS-level inspection (ptrace-equivalent) rather than injecting code -- no instrumentation, no restart, and it doesn't pause or measurably slow the target process for a dump.

flashcards.q: Why does py-spy NOT auto-detect deadlocks the way jstack does?
flashcards.a: The JVM has centralized, interpreter-level bookkeeping of synchronized monitor locks it can walk to detect a cycle; Python's threading.Lock has no equivalent centralized tracking a stack tool can query, so a human must manually cross-reference which locks each blocked thread waits on and who holds them.

flashcards.q: What is the core architectural difference between Parca and Pyroscope for continuous profiling, with overhead numbers?
flashcards.a: Parca uses eBPF at the kernel level, no per-language SDK needed, reported under 1% overhead. Pyroscope uses language-runtime sampling (~100Hz), needs a per-language agent, reported 1-3% overhead but with richer language-aware stack detail.

flashcards.q: Why is continuous profiling architecturally different from every other tool in this module?
flashcards.a: Core/thread/heap dumps and one-off py-spy runs are all point-in-time captures -- useless if you didn't capture at the right moment. Continuous profiling (Pyroscope/Parca) runs always-on so a retroactive query like 'what was CPU doing at 3am last Tuesday' is answerable without having predicted the incident in advance.

flashcards.q: Why should you never restart a hung process before attempting a dump?
flashcards.a: Restarting destroys the exact evidence (the process's current stack state) needed to diagnose the root cause. py-spy dump or jstack take milliseconds to seconds and cost essentially nothing, so capture should always precede restart.

flashcards.q: What is Eclipse MAT's recommended heap dump analysis workflow, in order?
flashcards.a: Leak Suspects Report (automated first pass) -> Histogram (which classes dominate) -> Dominator Tree (retained size, what's really retaining memory) -> Path to GC Roots (confirm the exact reference chain keeping an object alive).

flashcards.q: Why did full jmap heap dumps historically risk causing their own production incident?
flashcards.a: jmap -dump:live forces a full GC and, on older tooling especially, could pause application threads for the dump's duration -- a multi-GB heap dump can take real minutes, which is part of why jcmd is now the recommended lower-overhead alternative.
